### Question 1

Picture a garden hose that is already full of water. Each time the pump at one end squeezes, a small bulge races down the hose, and resting your fingers on the hose lets you feel that bulge pass. The heart is the pump, the arteries are the hose, and the bulge is the pulse. You are not feeling the heart itself, and you are not feeling the pressure inside the hose; you are feeling the wave that each contraction sends down the tubing. Because one squeeze makes one bulge, counting bulges normally tells you how often the heart is squeezing.

### Question 2

Treat 60 to 100 as the posted speed limits for a resting adult heart. Sixty is the low end and one hundred is the high end, and anything between them is ordinary cruising speed. The numbers are easy to anchor to a clock: about one beat per second at the bottom of the range and a little under two beats per second at the top. Children's hearts run faster because their bodies are smaller and their metabolisms are quicker, so they get their own set of posted limits rather than borrowing the adult ones.

### Question 3

The prefix tachy- comes from a Greek word meaning swift, and it survives in tachometer, the dial that shows how fast an engine is spinning. Brady- means slow. So tachycardia is a swift heart and bradycardia is a slow heart. Notice that both words describe only speed, not strength and not evenness. Amplitude and rhythm are answering different questions entirely, which is why a chart entry needs all three descriptions rather than a single number.

### Question 4

Your thumb carries a surprisingly loud pulse of its own. Press it against someone's wrist and you may end up counting yourself while believing you are counting them, rather like trying to hear a friend whisper while your own headphones are playing. The pads of the first two fingers are much quieter, so any thumping you feel there is genuinely coming from the patient. The rule is about whose heartbeat you are hearing, not about how hard you press.

### Question 5

The heart carries a built-in metronome, and two different hands can reach over and adjust it. The sympathetic hand is the accelerator and pushes the ticks closer together. The vagus nerve is the brake, and it works by releasing acetylcholine, which makes each pacemaker cell take longer to build up to its next firing. More vagal signal therefore means a longer gap between ticks, which you feel as a slower pulse. Remove both hands entirely and the metronome still ticks, just at its own untouched pace.

### Question 6

Picture someone knocking on a door. How many knocks land per minute is the rate. How hard each knock lands is the amplitude. Whether the knocks arrive evenly spaced or in a jumbled cluster is the rhythm. A person can knock quickly but softly, or slowly but forcefully, so knowing one of these tells you nothing reliable about the others. That independence is exactly why documentation asks for all three descriptions instead of a single number.

### Question 7

Chemical reactions speed up when things get warmer, and the heart's pacemaker is a chemical process. During a fever the body's cells burn fuel faster and demand more oxygen delivery, so circulation has to turn over more quickly to keep up. At the same time the pacemaker cells themselves are sitting in warmer tissue, so they build toward each firing faster, like a clock left in the sun that starts running ahead. Both effects push in the same direction, which is why a rising temperature and a rising pulse usually travel together.

### Question 8

If rain fell at a perfectly steady drizzle, you could measure fifteen seconds of it and multiply by four to get the minute. But when rain arrives in random bursts, the fifteen seconds you happened to sample might be a downpour or a dry spell, and multiplying carries that luck straight into your answer. An irregular pulse is bursty rain. The only way to know what actually fell is to hold the bucket out for the whole minute and count what lands in it.

### Question 9

Imagine two people bailing water from a boat. One has a small cup and must scoop rapidly; the other has a large bucket and finishes the same job with far fewer scoops. A trained athlete's heart is the large bucket, moving more blood with each contraction, so it can beat less often and still move the same total volume every minute. The number by itself is not the finding. What makes a low rate concerning is the company it keeps, such as dizziness, weakness, or fainting.

### Question 10

A baby's wrist pulse is tiny and very fast, rather like trying to feel a hummingbird's wingbeat through a mitten. Rather than guess at the wrist, you listen at the source with a stethoscope over the heart, which is the apical pulse. The general rule is to go to the source whenever the signal at the edge is too faint, too fast, or too irregular to trust. The one time you must stay at the edge is when the edge itself is what you are evaluating, such as circulation below a new cast.

### Question 11

Picture a drummer striking a drum while a friend across the room counts the beats they can feel through the floorboards. Every strike makes a sound, but the softest ones never carry far enough to shake the floor, so the friend's count comes up short. Each heart contraction makes a sound at the chest, yet the weakest ones do not push enough blood to raise a bump at the wrist. The difference between the two counts is the pulse deficit, and it tells you how many beats each minute are doing essentially no work.

### Question 12

Think of the arteries as a river system. The carotid is the wide main channel just downstream of the pump, while the radial is a narrow stream far out at the edge of the network. When the water level drops, the small stream runs dry first while the main channel is still flowing, which is why the neck is where you check when circulation is in question. But two neck channels feed the brain, and pressing both at once is like damming the brain's supply while you are trying to measure it, so you check one side, then the other.
